newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin reassures Russians he is in charge.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin reassures Russians he is in charge.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin hit back on Thursday at rivals who want him to resign because of ill health, saying he was firmly in charge and that it was too soon to take his picture down from office walls.

Speaking slowly but clearly in a six-minute radio address, apparently recorded in hospital, Yeltsin backed beleagured Alexander Lebed over a Chechen peace deal after the security tsar was jeered in parliament on Wednesday for signing it.

Yeltsin later discussed Chechnya with Lebed at the hospital where he is preparing for heart surgery and Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev started talks in Moscow to try to reinforce the August 31 peace agreement.

The 65-year-old president's main aim, both in his speech and by increasing his workload this week, seemed to be to reassure the nation of almost 150 million that he is in charge and well enough to have a bypass operation in six to 10 weeks.

"I am in touch with what is going on in the country. I am helped by a strong team of professionals," said Yeltsin, who had two heart attacks last year and has been in hospital awaiting the operation since September 13. Doctors say he may have had a third attack before the presidential election runoff.

Scoffing at talk that he was too ill to rule the country, he added: "I said before the elections and repeat now -- don't rush to change the portraits. The country has a president and an active president at that!"

Yeltsin played down talk of chaos in the Kremlin since he disappeared from public view just before his reelection on July 3. Attacks by his opponents, who say he should step down, reached a peak in parliament on Wednesday.

Responding to talk of a power struggle in his absence, Yeltsin signalled his approval of the work of the three main potential rivals -- Lebed, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Anatoly Chubais, head of the Kremlin administration.
He saved particular praise for Lebed, whom he brought into his team after the former paratroop general came third in the first round of the presidential election on June 16.
"My aide Alexander Lebed fulfilled my instruction and stopped the military conflict (in Chechnya)," Yeltsin said, adding that a lot still had to be done to implement the deal.
Yeltsin also expressed concern about the state of the army and met Defence Minister Igor Rodionov to discuss financing of the armed forces.
He said in the radio address that a meeting of defence officials to be chaired by Chernomyrdin on Friday should come up with "concrete decisions" on the future of the army.
"I am very worried about the situation in the armed forces ...this situation must not be dragged out any longer," he said.

He said parliament's main task in the coming weeks was to approve the 1997 budget and identified Chechnya as Russia's biggest problem. Tens of thousands of people have been killed there since Russia sent troops in in December 1994.
A ceasefire agreed on August 31 has held, but a planned Russian troop withdrawal is proceeding slowly. Prisoner exchanges have also not gone as well as planned.
Yandarbiyev flew to Moscow on Thursday for talks intended to help implement the deal. He began his meetings by holding talks with Russian Nationalities Minister Vyacheslav Mikhailov.

In separate comments, Yeltsin commemorated the third anniversary of a hardline uprising in Moscow in which he used tanks to put down a rebellion by parliamentarians. Weeks before, Yeltsin had overturned the constitution and dissolved the legislature, accusing it of blocking reforms.
About 140 people were killed in clashes.
"Let us do everything to...ensure that those tragic events never happen in our land again," he said.
Opposition rallies were expected in Moscow later on Thursday to mark the 1993 events.
